summary: Acts resumes Luke's story during the forty days after Jesus's resurrection. Jesus teaches about God's kingdom, tells the apostles to wait in Jerusalem for the promised Holy Spirit, and redirects their question about Israel's restoration toward a vocation: Spirit-empowered witness from Jerusalem through Judea and Samaria to the earth's farthest reach. After Jesus is taken from their sight, the Galilean followers return from the Mount of Olives, pray with the women, Mary, and Jesus's brothers, and restore the symbolic Twelve by choosing Matthias to replace Judas.
whyItMatters: The opening supplies the program for the whole book. Mission is neither imperial expansion nor human self-assertion; witnesses receive power, cross inherited boundaries, and testify to the risen Jesus while the timetable remains God's. The community begins not by rushing outward but by waiting, praying, reading Scripture, facing Judas's loss, and repairing its leadership.

context.author: The anonymous author of Luke's Gospel, traditionally identified as Luke, addressing Theophilus in a second volume
context.audience: Theophilus and later readers learning how the Jesus movement traveled from Jerusalem toward Rome
context.date: Debated; commonly placed in the late first century
context.setting: Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives between resurrection and Pentecost
context.literaryForm: Secondary preface, commission scene, ascension narrative, community summary, and leadership-restoration account

outline.heading: The risen Jesus promises the Spirit and commissions witnesses
Jesus departs and the apostles return to Jerusalem
Peter interprets Judas's vacancy and Matthias is chosen

keyVerses.text: But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.”
keyVerses.why: This is Acts' geographic and theological program: received power becomes boundary-crossing witness.

keyVerses.text: who also said, “You men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into the sky? This Jesus, who was received up from you into the sky, will come back in the same way as you saw him going into the sky.”
keyVerses.why: Hope for Jesus's return turns the disciples from passive staring toward their present commission.

keyVerses.text: They prayed and said, “You, Lord, who know the hearts of all men, show which one of these two you have chosen
keyVerses.why: The restored community combines discernment, named qualifications, prayer, and acknowledged dependence on God.

questions.question: What does the Greek word for ‘witnesses’ imply?
questions.answer: Martyres are people who attest what they know; here the apostles have encountered the risen Jesus and are commissioned to testify about him. The word later becomes associated with dying for one's testimony, giving English ‘martyr,’ but 1:8 primarily names their vocation, not a command to seek death. Acts will widen the witnessing circle while repeatedly joining testimony to the Spirit's power.

questions.question: Does Jesus reject Israel's restoration in verse 7?
questions.answer: No. The apostles ask ‘at this time,’ and Jesus says that the times belong to the Father's authority; he redirects them to their task rather than declaring Israel irrelevant. The route begins in Jerusalem, includes Judea and Samaria, and moves to the nations. Acts continues to speak of Israel's hope, so Gentile mission should not be read as God's contempt for Jewish people.

questions.question: Where is ‘the uttermost parts of the earth’?
questions.answer: The Greek phrase eschatou tēs gēs can mean the earth's farthest reach and echoes Isaiah's servant mission. Readers propose Rome, Spain, Ethiopia, or the whole inhabited world, but Acts never pins it to one map coordinate. Rome is the book's narrative destination, not the mission's final boundary; the phrase makes Jerusalem the point from which witness keeps radiating.

questions.question: What does the ascension claim—and what does ‘sky’ language do?
questions.answer: Luke narrates Jesus being taken from ordinary sight and exalted to God's sphere; cloud language evokes divine presence rather than a claim that heaven is merely a location above the atmosphere. The two figures promise continuity between the departing and returning Jesus. Their question also prevents the scene from becoming an invitation to calculate or stare instead of witness.

questions.question: Who belongs to the waiting community?
questions.answer: Luke names the eleven, women who had followed Jesus, Mary his mother, and his brothers. The plural ‘women’ matters: the community is broader than the apostolic list, and women have already been resurrection witnesses in Luke. Their repeated action is homothymadon—being together with one purpose—in persistent prayer, not leaderless inactivity.

questions.question: Why do Acts and Matthew describe Judas's death differently?
questions.answer: Acts emphasizes the field, Judas's fall, and the gruesome public result; Matthew emphasizes hanging himself and the priests' purchase. Readers propose ways the accounts could describe stages of one event, while others see distinct early traditions shaped for different narrative purposes. Acts itself focuses on the vacancy Judas left and the community's scriptural response, not a medical reconstruction.

questions.question: What is Akeldama, and why does Luke translate it?
questions.answer: Akeldama is an Aramaic place-name meaning ‘Field of Blood.’ Luke supplies its meaning for Greek readers who may not know Jerusalem's Semitic speech. The gloss is a small reminder that Acts is written in Greek while its opening world is multilingual and deeply Jewish.

questions.question: Was casting lots a careless substitute for discernment?
questions.answer: The group first identifies an apostolic qualification—continuous presence from John's baptism through the ascension—then presents two eligible men and prays to the heart-knowing Lord. Casting lots has biblical precedent for receiving a decision believed to be God's. Acts does not prescribe it as the normal later method; after the Spirit comes, leadership discernment takes several forms.

glossary.def: The named recipient of Luke and Acts; the Greek name means ‘friend of God’ or ‘loved by God,’ but it can be an ordinary personal name.
A conventional limited travel distance associated with Sabbath observance; Luke uses it to locate the Mount of Olives near Jerusalem.
A commissioned ‘sent one’; in this scene the restored Twelve have a distinctive eyewitness qualification.
